title: Small World Animal Habitats
strapline: Four trays, four worlds — desert, forest, Arctic and sea — and the right animal for each.
intent: Children build an understanding of where different animals live and why.
Matching animal to habitat is real classification: sorting by a rule that means something.
Handling contrasting materials — sand, leaves, ice, water — grounds the learning in the senses.
Explaining a choice out loud turns a sorting decision into reasoning.
Small world play invites sustained, narrative play that children return to over days.
implementation: Set out trays with materials for different habitats: sand for desert, leaves for forest, ice cubes or cotton wool for Arctic, a water tray for sea.
Add animal figures that genuinely belong in each, plus a few that do not, to provoke discussion.
Model sorting animals into the correct habitats, thinking aloud as you do it.
Introduce the vocabulary in play — jungle, ocean, desert, cold, hot, dry, wet.
Ask children to explain their choices rather than correcting a wrong one straight away.
Leave the trays out across the half-term so play can develop rather than being a one-off.
Add books and photographs of the real habitats alongside the trays.
key_questions: Where do you think this animal lives? What makes you say that?
What would happen if the polar bear went in the desert tray?
How does this habitat feel different from that one?
Which animals could live in more than one of our trays?
What else does this animal need in its home?

impact.text: Children make connections between animals and the environments they live in.
Children sort and match by a real rule and notice same and different.
Children explain their thinking and negotiate with others in play.
Children take up new vocabulary from the topic and use it in their own play.
Children sustain imaginative play with shared storylines and roles.
Children ask real questions about the world and expect real answers.

enhancements: A world map on the wall with each habitat tray pegged to where it is.
A cold-hands investigation of the Arctic tray with real ice and thermometers.
A child-built habitat — let them design and stock a fifth tray themselves.
A non-fiction book basket beside the trays for checking a claim.
A "what would you need?" challenge — pack a bag for a trip to each habitat.
A camouflage extension linking to the Animal Patterns Art card.

playing_exploring: Children explore contrasting materials and figures with no fixed outcome.
The trays invite open-ended small world narrative play.
active_learning: Children return to the trays across days, developing the play further each time.
They concentrate for long stretches on building and rebuilding a world.
creating_thinking: Children classify by a real rule and defend their choices.
They predict what would happen if an animal were in the wrong place.
